en: Watch a price rise in one neighborhood spread to its neighbors, and change the loan cap and a rate shock. A toy model, not investment advice.

Does a price rise that starts in one neighborhood spread to its neighbors? Change how strongly people follow recent gains next door (price contagion), the loan cap and a rate shock, and watch 900 neighborhoods on a grid. It is a toy model of the structure, not a picture of any real area.
Each cell of a 30×30 grid is a neighborhood, and every price index starts at 100. One step is one quarter. The rise starts in the central 7×7 block (dashed square).
Each neighborhood's growth combines its own recent gains (momentum), the recent gains of its 8 neighbors (price contagion), the expectation that prices keep rising, and small random shocks.

There is an "income line" that rises slowly with incomes, and a higher loan cap lets prices climb further above it (the affordability ceiling). Above the ceiling growth is dragged down; below the line buyers return.
If you choose a rate shock, from that quarter the ceiling drops and expectations sour, so prices cool.

④ Stronger Contagion, Looser Lending

The horizontal axis is price contagion; the vertical axis is the highest share of overvalued neighborhoods during the run. Compare what changes when only the loan cap is lowered to 40% at the same contagion. Dots are 5 runs.
Your loan cap
Loan cap 40%

What it shows: In this model, up to a contagion of 0.4 the rise barely spreads (at most about 8% of neighborhoods overvalued); at 0.5 about 90% become overvalued, and from 0.6 up it reaches every neighborhood. At the same contagion, lowering the loan cap to 40% left almost no spread. With the default settings (contagion 0.6, loan cap 60%, a rate shock at quarter 50), the average price rose to about 230 and then fell about 24% from its peak. The structure of following each other can matter more for how a rise spreads than the circumstances of any one neighborhood.

What it doesn't show: This is not a price forecast for any real city or area, and it is not advice on investing or property transactions. The model has no supply, population, taxes, financial regulation or policy, and its numbers (contagion strength, loan cap, size of the rate shock) are chosen to show structure, so they cannot be compared directly with real markets.

A toy model built on the idea of herding, being drawn by neighbors' recent gains, and on spatial diffusion models. It draws inspiration from Shiller's work on how market sentiment and narratives move prices, but it does not reproduce any specific paper or real data; it is this project's own design.

Growth = 0.30 × (own previous growth) + contagion × (average of 8 neighbors) + 0.004 × optimism + a random shock (SD 0.6%). The ceiling = income line × (loan cap ÷ 0.4)<sup>1.5</sup>; above the ceiling growth is reduced by 25% of the log gap, and below the income line it is raised by the same amount. Income grows 0.5% per quarter.

A rate shock cuts the ceiling by 30% from that quarter, reduces optimism to a quarter, and adds a downward pressure (up to −1.2%) that fades over 12 quarters. All these constants were chosen arbitrarily.
"Overvalued" in graphs ③ and ④ means priced more than 30% above the income line. Graph ④ runs 80 quarters 5 times each without a rate shock. You can verify with node tools/validate-apartment.js.
The code is available on GitHub.
Why Does Winning an Auction Cost You? · Simulatio Lab
Run the winner's curse yourself and see why the highest bidder in a painting auction loses money on average.

Nobody knows a painting's true value, and each bidder holds a slightly wrong estimate. The highest bidder wins the auction, but is that really good news? Change the number of bidders, the estimation error and how much people shade their bids.
The painting's true value V is the same for everyone but unknown (random between 70 and 130 in each auction). Each bidder receives an estimate of V with some error added.
Everyone bids "estimate − shading × size of the error". With shading at 0, they simply bid their estimate.
The highest bid wins. The price is the winner's own bid in the first-price rule, and the second-highest bid in the second-price rule.
The winner's profit is the true value minus the price paid (values average 100). If everyone shades by the same amount, the winner stays the same and only the price drops.
Number of bidders <output id="o-n"></output>
With more bidders, someone is more likely to overestimate badly
Estimation error <output id="o-sigma"></output>
In % of the value. Larger means less accurate estimates
